newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai sugar premiums ease in listless market.
newsitem.headline: Thai sugar premiums ease in listless market.

text.p: Thai raw sugar premiums eased in the past week as physical demand waned and the market was rife with bearish news, trade sources said on Monday.
"We have not heard of any new orders. The market is quiet at the end of the season," one trader said.
January/March delivery was bid at around 0.92-0.95 cent a pound over New York futures from about 1.00 cent a pound last week. March/May delivery was bid at 0.78-0.80 cent a pound over New York March.

Sentiment was dampened by analysts' forecasts that world sugar prices would drop under the weight of a 1996/97 surplus and rising stocks and news that the Phillipines was unlikely to import sugar in the next six months because it had overbought.

The International Sugar Organization on Friday forecast that world sugar prices would drift lower towards a long-term average of 10 cents a pound due to a projected sugar surplus of 2.5 million tonnes for 1996/97. World prices for raw sugar are currently hovering around 10.80 cents/lb in New York.
Many traders said they did not think the downward revision of 1996/97 (November-October) Thai sugar cane output released by the agriculture ministry on Monday would help support the premiums.
The ministry cut its sugar cane output projection to 61.53 million tonnes from 62.42 tonnes earlier due to floods which ravaged many parts of Thailand after the monsoon season started late May.
"The drop is not significant. I wouldn't expect it to push the premiums up, at least not much," said a trader from a Japanese trading house.
In a related development, the Industry Ministry announced that the sugar cane crushing for this season would start on November 5, but only for the 11 mills in northeastern region.
The crushing schedules for central, northern and eastern areas will be decided later this month, a ministry official said.
At Thai port, Kerry bought 2,300 tonnes of white sugar to be shipped to Indonesia. The vessel Bangpo arrived for loading on October 16 and was scheduled to leave the port Monday.
Sangthai Radium left Bangkok port on October 15 for Singapore with 1,000 tonnes of white sugar. Tate & Lyle was the buyer.
